rows.grounds: topic of the path of space

items.question: How is the method of the path of space presented in this teaching?
premises: The path of space is now being taught.
It is presented through contraction and expansion.
This method is seen in the Shaiva scriptures.
items.inference: The teaching of the path of space follows a scriptural method of contraction and expansion.
items.plain_english: Now the method of the path of space is sung in brief and in detail, as it is taught in the Shaiva scriptures.

rows.grounds: nature of the path of time
origin of the path of space

items.question: What is the relationship between the path of time and the path of space?
premises: The path of time has already been examined.
The path of time is made of the Lord's power of action.
The path of space arises from the variety of forms and from that.
items.inference: After explaining the time-path rooted in action, the text now explains the space-path rooted in the variety of forms.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'born from that' is slightly compressed in the compound.
items.plain_english: The path of time, which consists of the Lord's power of action, has already been examined; now the path of space, born from the variety of forms and from that, is explained.

rows.grounds: unreality of what is not grounded

items.question: Where is the entire path ultimately established?
premises: This whole path is established in consciousness alone.
Anything not resting in consciousness lacks real grounding.
What lacks such grounding is like a flower in the sky.
items.inference: The entire path of space has reality only insofar as it rests in consciousness.
items.plain_english: This entire path is established in pure consciousness alone; whatever does not rest there is no more real than a flower in the sky.

items.question: Through what levels does the path of space become established?
premises: The path is manifested through consciousness.
It appears in the void, intellect, vital airs, and channel networks.
Its outer abiding is in the external body.
items.inference: The path of space unfolds from consciousness through inner levels and finally abides in the outer body.
items.plain_english: Manifested through consciousness, the path abides in the void, in the intellect, in the vital airs, in the networks of channels, and outwardly in the body.

items.question: Why should the yogi discern the path of space in this way?
premises: The path is to be discerned in its proper order.
The yogi can continually attend to that order.
Such attention leads quickly to the state of Bhairava.
items.inference: Careful contemplation of the path's order enables the yogi to attain Bhairava swiftly.
items.plain_english: The yogi should discern the path in this way, for by continually attending to its proper order he quickly attains the state of Bhairava.

items.question: What happens when consciousness abides pervading all objects by the mere desire to see?
premises: Consciousness can abide pervading all objects.
This can occur through the mere desire to see.
The Spanda teaching says no further elaboration is needed then.
items.inference: When pervading awareness is present, elaborate explanation becomes unnecessary.
items.plain_english: When, by the mere desire to see, consciousness abides pervading all objects, what more needs to be said? So it is taught in the Spanda scripture.

items.question: How should the yogi dissolve the entire path in contemplative practice?
premises: The yogi first knows the entire path.
The path is dissolved into its ruling lords.
Those lords are then dissolved into body, breath, and mind in order.
items.inference: Contemplation proceeds by knowing the path and dissolving it step by step into subtler supports.
items.plain_english: Having known the entire path, one should dissolve it into its lords, and then dissolve those lords, in due order, into the circle of body, breath, and mind, as taught before.

items.question: What is the effect of dissolving everything into one's own consciousness?
premises: The whole path is dissolved into one's own consciousness.
That consciousness is full and self-sufficient.
When contemplated, it destroys transmigratory bondage.
items.inference: Contemplation of one's own full consciousness dissolves the ocean of samsara.
items.plain_english: All of that should be dissolved into one's own consciousness; when that consciousness, full in its own nature, is contemplated, it becomes the fire that consumes the ocean of transmigration.

items.question: Which lords rule which ranges of the path according to the Mrikshottara?
premises: The Mrikshottara teaches the lords of the path.
Vishnu rules from Ananta up to Pradhana.
The next range extends from Purusha up to Kala.
items.inference: The scripture assigns specific cosmic ranges to specific lords of the path.
uncertainties: The verse breaks mid-list; the lord of the Purusha-to-Kala range is completed in the next verse.
items.plain_english: In the revered Mrikshottara, the teacher declared these lords of the path: Vishnu rules from Ananta up to Pradhana, and the next range runs from Purusha up to Kala.

items.question: How does the hierarchy of path-lords culminate in the supreme Shiva?
premises: Rudra and Isha rule specific intermediate ranges.
The unsupported Shiva pervades the Sadakhya sphere.
Beyond that pervading Shiva is the supreme who pervades even him.
items.inference: The cosmic hierarchy of lords resolves into the supreme Shiva who pervades all levels.
uncertainties: The phrase 'in the knot' is terse and may refer to a specific transitional boundary in the tattva scheme.
items.plain_english: Rudra rules in the knot, Isha in Maya, and the unsupported Shiva in the sphere of Sadakhya; beyond that, the supreme is the pervader of even that Shiva.

items.question: What kind of knowledge is affirmed in the Svacchanda teaching regarding attainment of Shiva-hood?
premises: One may understand oneself as having attained Shiva-hood.
The Svacchanda teaching addresses this realization.
It states that such knowledge is not merely procedural.
items.inference: True knowledge of Shiva-hood transcends mere ritual or procedural technique.
items.plain_english: Thus, in the Svacchanda teaching it is explained that realizing 'I have attained Shiva-hood' is not a knowledge that depends merely on procedure.

items.question: How does the Trishiras teaching describe awareness and differentiation?
premises: The Trishiras teaching divides awareness into root, middle, and tip.
The thirty-six principles unfold within this framework.
Memory constructs differentiation.
items.inference: Differentiated cosmic structure is presented as a conceptual unfolding within awareness shaped by memory.
items.plain_english: In the Trishiras teaching, awareness is conceived as root, middle, and tip; the unfolding of the thirty-six principles is there, and memory is what constructs difference.

items.question: What characterizes the root level of awareness in this teaching?
premises: The root of awareness is an 'I am' state with unobstructed division.
It contains the state of all principles.
Yet in one's own self it remains without division.
items.inference: At the root level, all principles are present in awareness without actual fragmentation.
items.plain_english: The root of awareness is the 'I am' state in which division is unobstructed; it is the state of all principles, yet in one's own self it remains undivided.

items.question: How is the middle level of awareness distinguished from the root?
premises: The middle of awareness shows some relation of support and supported.
It arises through division among the principles.
It is marked by things abiding in their own nature.
items.inference: The middle level is where differentiated principles appear as relatively stable and relational.
items.plain_english: The middle level of awareness is marked by a certain relation of support and supported; through the division of the principles, things appear as abiding in their own distinct natures.

items.question: What defines the highest or tip level of awareness?
premises: The tip of awareness is pure knowing.
It is waveless and vast bliss.
It brings past, future, and worlds into oneness with consciousness.
items.inference: The highest level of awareness is a blissful, still unity that gathers all manifestations into consciousness.
uncertainties: The compound at the end is compact; 'worlds/cities' is an interpretive rendering of purādika.
items.plain_english: The tip of awareness is pure knowing, waveless and vast bliss, bringing past, future, and all worlds into oneness with consciousness.

items.question: How is the supreme reality identified in the Deviyayamala citation?
premises: Unbroken consciousness is identified as Bhairava.
Bhairava is the supreme Lord.
The Deviyayamala speaks of the path adorned by the thirty-six principles.
items.inference: The supreme Lord is unbroken consciousness, within which the thirty-sixfold path is beautifully displayed.
uncertainties: The exact title form 'Deviyayamala' follows the transmitted reading; standardization varies.
items.plain_english: Unbroken consciousness is Bhairava, the supreme Lord; and in the revered Deviyayamala the path is described as beautiful with the thirty-six principles.

items.question: What is the effect of meditating on the sixfold path, given the Lord's nondual nature?
premises: Meditating on the sixfold path makes one become Shiva.
The Lord is not different from consciousness.
The concession introduces an apparent tension with spatial divisions.
items.inference: Meditation on the sixfold path leads to Shiva-identity even though the Lord transcends real spatial division.
items.plain_english: By meditating on the sixfold path one immediately becomes Shiva, even though that Lord, not different from consciousness, has no real divisions.

items.question: If the full Lord has no real spatial divisions, why speak of them?
premises: The full Lord has no real above, beginning, middle, or end.
Teaching still addresses learners and teachers.
Pedagogical needs can justify provisional divisions.
items.inference: Spatial divisions are not ultimately real but are used for the sake of teaching and understanding.
items.plain_english: For that full reality there is no real arrangement of above, beginning, middle, or end; even so, such divisions are used for the sake of those who learn and those who teach.

items.question: Why is the earthly principle treated as the lowest or innermost level?
premises: Divisions like middle and so on are conceived according to one's own nature.
These divisions are limited by the knower's conception.
Tradition identifies the earthly principle accordingly.
items.inference: The placement of the earthly principle is a pedagogical convention shaped by the knower's conceptual limits.
items.plain_english: Conceptions such as middle and so forth arise according to one's own nature; therefore, by the limitation of the knower's conception, they designate the earthly principle as such.

items.question: What is described within the earthly principle in this section?
premises: The earthly principle is treated as surrounded by all coverings.
It is taken as a central reference point in the exposition.
The text now turns to the arrangement of worlds within it.
items.inference: The discussion now begins the cosmological account of worlds located in the earthly principle.
items.plain_english: That principle, standing amid all and covered by all the enveloping layers, is now described in terms of the arrangement of worlds within the earthly principle.

items.question: Who rules the Kataha Rudras in the lower cosmology described here?
premises: The Kataha Rudras are devoted to desire.
Their ruler is Ananta.
He is depicted mounted on a vessel within the waters, reeling from drink.
items.inference: Ananta is presented as the lord of the desire-driven Kataha Rudras in the lower waters.
items.plain_english: Ananta is the ruler of the Kataha Rudras, who are devoted to desire; he is depicted mounted on a vessel within the waters, reeling from drinking liquor.

items.question: Where is the world of Kalagni located in relation to Ananta?
premises: Ananta meditates on Bhairava and is surrounded by serpents.
Above him is the world of Kalagni.
That world is raised to a height of one crore of yojanas.
items.inference: The cosmology places Kalagni's world above Ananta at a vast measured height.
items.plain_english: Meditating on the god Bhairava and surrounded by serpents, he is below the world of Kalagni, which rises above to a height of ten million yojanas.

items.question: Why does Ananta not look upward toward the world of Kalagni?
premises: The worlds fear being reduced to ashes by Kalagni.
Ananta does not look upward.
Although he pervades the universe, Kalagni threatens to burn this earth.
items.inference: Even a pervasive cosmic lord avoids looking toward Kalagni because of its destructive fire.
items.plain_english: He does not look upward, for fear that the worlds would be reduced to ashes; and although he pervades the universe, he avoids that direction because Kalagni would scorch this earth.

items.question: How are the distances around Kalagni's world measured in this cosmology?
premises: Kalagni is placed below the hells because of its manifest fire.
Its flame extends ten crores of yojanas.
Above it there is an empty space of half that measure.
items.inference: The text gives precise vertical measures locating Kalagni below the hells with flame below and void above.
items.plain_english: Because it is manifest before the hells, that world is placed below them; the mighty one's flame extends ten crores of yojanas, and above it there is an empty space of half that extent.
